title: Ollama and Fly.io Sprites: cloud model access without copying keys into agent computers
summary: A documented gateway keeps an Ollama API key outside the agent’s Linux environment. Default-denied policies and separate compute and inference billing make this useful for bounded app and teaching workflows.

sections.title: Give an agent a computer without copying its model key into it
sections.html:
Ollama’s October 13 announcement adds a connector to Fly.io Sprites: persistent hosted Linux environments that can call cloud models without possessing the provider’s long-lived API key. This separates the working environment from one credential; it does not make every agent action harmless.

The Ollama walkthrough describes adding a key to a Fly.io organization and granting selected Sprites access. Current Fly documentation explains identity checks and default denial. This is remote execution paired with Ollama Cloud inference, so offline operation, local-model privacy and free inference should not be inferred from the Ollama name.

sections.title: Follow the request and the authority
sections.html:
The provider key stays in encrypted organization-level storage. A Sprite receives a connection identifier and gateway URL. Fly identifies the caller, checks policy and forwards the request with the stored credential attached. Ollama’s example omits the Authorization header; its Python example supplies an unused placeholder key because the gateway performs authentication. An authorized agent can still consume inference or send sensitive data in prompts. Credential possession, permission to invoke a provider and access to source data are separate concerns.

Connections deny all Sprites initially. Policies can select a name prefix and labels; when combined, both conditions apply. Allow-all overrides narrower conditions. A classroom project could use a dedicated prefix and label, but that configuration alone does not prevent misuse.

Provider-path allow- and block-lists support exact paths and trailing-wildcard prefixes, with blocks taking precedence. Configuration currently requires the API rather than the dashboard. These controls restrict paths; the documentation does not establish per-model restrictions inside request bodies or per-student token budgets. Application limits and provider account controls remain necessary.

sections.title: A small first trial has a clear result
sections.html:
Prerequisites are an Ollama API key, a Fly.io organization and a Sprite. An authorized administrator configures access and tests reachability. A proposed disposable trial should use synthetic text and a tiny program: confirm denial before granting access, verify one short request after granting it, then revoke eligibility and check denial again. Preserve expected and observed results.

A 403 can indicate a Sprite lacks permission or a provider path is blocked. A gateway 401 can indicate invalid Fly identity headers. Requests must originate inside a running Sprite, not a laptop or ordinary CI process; replacing the provider key would not fix that location error.

Test the exact SDK, agent and endpoint intended for deployment. The documented examples do not establish compatibility with every streaming mode, tool-calling convention or SDK version. No connector or model request was executed for this report.

sections.title: An educational programming lab with controlled model access
sections.html:
A practical teaching exercise adapts Ollama’s fuzzing example to a deliberately constrained parser. Give each team the same disposable program, tests and synthetic fixtures. One model proposes malformed inputs; the Sprite runs them; another model explains failures. Students verify those explanations against actual test results. Preserve code, inputs and observed output so the class can reproduce the exercise.

Persistent files support iterative lessons but also preserve mistakes. Keep a known starting point and explicit reset procedure. Fly describes checkpoints as restoring filesystem contents, not resuming a paused process mid-instruction, so verify that the application restarts after restoration.

Keep submitted work, generated suggestions and test results distinguishable. Assessment should require passing specified cases and explaining failures. An agent’s completion message does not establish correctness; the instructor still supplies the rubric.

sections.title: Use the environment around a concrete application
sections.html:
An application worker can accept an authorized task, call a model, run deterministic validation and return a result for review. The application must maintain job states, retry limits and deduplication: the connector does not supply them. An interrupted worker could otherwise repeat an expensive request.

For websites, Fly describes a per-Sprite HTTPS URL that wakes the environment on request, with a service listening on port 8080. Private organizational access and public exposure are separate settings. Choose deliberately who can open a prototype; an outbound model connector does not control inbound application access.

For video teams, an agent could propose chapters and candidate clips from a transcript and edit decision list. Code should validate filenames, segment existence and timings against source duration; a human editor approves selection and meaning. Keep footage and approved cuts under team control. This produces a reviewable handoff for an educational video or product demo, but the integration does not establish native video generation, GPU rendering or compatibility with a particular nonlinear editor. The editor can correct an individual selection without rerunning the whole generative production pipeline.

sections.title: Budget the computer and the model separately
sections.html:
On October 28, the Sprites product page displayed $0.0385 per CPU-hour, $0.021875 per GB-hour of memory, and hot/cold storage rates of $0.000683/$0.000027 per GB-hour. One CPU-hour plus two GB-hours of memory totals $0.08225 before storage and inference. This illustrates units, not measured task consumption. Idle environments stop accruing compute charges while storage remains billed. Trial-credit eligibility was not checked. Measure active time and storage before estimating a class or production workload; occasional activity differs from a continuously busy worker.

Ollama pricing separately lists pay-as-you-go cloud usage without a subscription and three concurrent requests. Observed input/cached-input/output prices per million tokens were $1.40/$0.26/$4.40 for GLM-5.3 and $3.00/$0.30/$15.00 for Kimi K3. These are snapshot prices for models in the integration examples. Context reuse, response length and repeated agent turns affect bills.

This connector uses an Ollama key you supply. Fly’s managed-provider arrangement mentions OpenRouter; do not assume its included usage or consolidated billing applies to Ollama. Confirm provider plans, budgets and model terms before scaling. Access to an open-weight model service does not itself license redistribution of every model’s weights.

sections.title: A useful boundary, with a testable scope
sections.html:
The integration offers a documented credential boundary and persistent execution environment. Its usefulness depends on explicit permissions and an inspectable application workflow.

This scan did not test isolation, credential leakage, revocation latency, checkpoint recovery, SDK behavior, billing or model quality. A narrow trial with synthetic data and measured usage is the next useful step. Educational labs, application workers and editorial assistants can evaluate whether removing repeated key distribution improves their workflow without mistaking that boundary for complete system reliability.

useCases: Agent-assisted programming labs with synthetic fixtures
Contained application workers with centrally configured model access
Transcript and edit-list preparation for human video editors
limitations: No connector, account, agent, checkpoint or paid inference tested.
Credential isolation does not prevent authorized misuse or inference spending.
Provider-path policy is not documented as per-model or per-student budgeting.
Cloud inference and persistent storage have separate costs; model licenses remain model-specific.

judgment: A practical infrastructure integration for teams already building agents. It deserves a small access-and-recovery trial; documentation alone does not establish end-to-end safety or production reliability.
researchNote: Oldest assigned backlog reconsidered before report selection. October 13 launch article and current primary docs/prices inspected in Chrome October 28. No installs, model calls, account changes or native testing performed. Educational, application and video examples are proposed workflows.
